catalog_quote: Sochiapam Chinantec has seven tones and two types of syllable stress, so there is the possibility of 14 tone-stress contrasts on any monosyllabic word. The consonant-vowel combination of ta, for example, has the following meanings. ¹ is used to mark high tone, ² = mid tone, ³ = low tone, double numbers such as ¹³ indicate a tone glide from one level to the other. Ballistic syllable stress (intense and short) is indicated by accent on the nuclear vowel, controlled syllable stress (low-intensity and long) is unmarked. ta¹ will we arrive? tá¹ complete (adjective) ta² we arrive (habitually) tá² recently ta³ foot tá³ weaving (noun) ta¹³ let's fight tá¹³ I will chop ... Whistle speech, based on 31 etic tone-stress distinctions, is used by men to communicate complex messages with minimal ambiguity. ... Verbs are marked by change in tone, stress, or vowels, or a combination of these for person …

audit.recode_to: Pending Foris 2000 Phonology chapter: if it states that the (final) root syllable bears stress and prefixal/pretonic syllables are unstressed (the pattern coded for Lealao and Ojitlan Chinantec), recode from 'tonal, domain UNSTATED' to the corresponding positional class (morphological/root or final) with tone + ballistic/controlled type retained in the note; if it states no word-level prominence beyond the syllable-type contrast, keep 'tonal' and upgrade the citation to the grammar with page.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote confirmed verbatim in the held SIL-Mexico page (Wayback 2007 capture and live copy), section 'Linguistic aspects of Sochiapam Chinantec'; Foris 1980 fn.2 (held scanned) corroborates. (2) The deciding source is a 2007 publisher web profile (author-signed) that describes tone x ballistic/controlled contrasts on monosyllables only; it is not the best available description. Glottolog lists Foris 2000 (xiii+407 pp, grammar) / Foris 1993 PhD (xxiii+584 pp) and Foris 1973 IJAL (phonology at syllable level); SIL's own ToC (opened today) shows a Phonology chapter and the blurb confirms polysyllabic words exist. sources.quote: 'Speakers of the language can use more than thirty tone-stress distinctions to communicate messages in whistle speech ... The majority of words consist of a single syllable; there are a small number of two-syllable words and less than a dozen known tri-syllabics. This model-neutral presentation describes everything from the phonemes up through phrases ... from the changes of tone and stress to changes in nucleus to signal a wide variety of tense, aspect, and related features.'
